title: The Maqsura of Ibn Durayd
intro: Ibn Durayd wrote this poem for the two Mikali emirs who had put him in charge of the chancery of Fars; al-Mas'udi, as Ibn Khallikan quotes him, names them as Abd Allah ibn Muhammad ibn Mikal and his son Abu al-Abbas Isma'il, and Ibn Khallikan says they rewarded him with ten thousand dirhams. It opens on grey hair, exile and a quarrel with Time, then takes comfort from kings whom death cut off short of their hopes, such as Imru' al-Qays, Jadhima and Yazid ibn al-Muhallab, and from those who did take their revenge, such as Amr ibn Adi and Sayf ibn Dhi Yazan; it swears by the pilgrims' camels, by war-horses and by the nobles of the poet's Yemeni kin, describes his sword and his horse, and turns to Iraq, the two emirs and a prayer for rain over Basra. Long runs of maxims on Time and people follow, then night journeys, a deserted well, a lookout and a dream-visitor that finds him in Fars, and the poem closes on old wine and his own resolve. Al-Mas'udi, again in Ibn Khallikan, reports the claim that Ibn Durayd gathered into it most of the maqsur, the nouns that end in an alif with no hamza after it, and Ibn Khallikan adds that a host of scholars, early and late, wrote commentaries on it and discussed its words.

translation: O gazelle, likest of all things to the wild cow,
grazing lavender among the trees of the dunes:
1.sharh: He addresses a woman as a gazelle that most resembles the wild cow, the classic image for large dark eyes. Al-Lakhmi says this line is missing from most transmissions; for most, the poem begins with the next.

translation: If you see my head, its colour now like
the edge of dawn beneath the trailing skirts of night,
2.sharh: The first grey hairs in his black hair are dawn's first light under night's hem. The “if” is not answered until line 9: everything he has suffered can be forgiven.

translation: and the white has caught fire in its black
as fire catches in thick ghada wood,
3.sharh: Grey hair spread through the black like fire through firewood. The verb echoes the Quran, where Zachariah says his head “has caught fire with grey”; ghada is a desert tree whose embers burn long.

translation: till it was like a jet-black night when the light
of morning settles in its corners, and it clears.
4.sharh: The same picture taken further: his head is a night going grey at the edges until the dark is gone. Ibn Khalawayh's text lacks this line; al-Lakhmi traces it to al-Farazdaq.

translation: And Time has drained the water of my vigour,
Time that shot the thoughts of my heart with burning grief.
5.sharh: Age has dried up the energy of his youth, and the same Time has wounded his thoughts with the torment of love and sorrow.

translation: The meadow of my pleasures has turned dry and withered
that once ran over with moist earth.
6.sharh: His youth was a lush meadow; now it is parched. Al-Lakhmi reads it as an old man looking back on the green days of his boyhood.

translation: Distance that scatters friends has lit an ember
that never lets up scorching the folds of my insides.
7.sharh: Separation from those he loves has left a live coal inside him that never stops burning. Arabic poetry feels longing in the bowels and liver as much as in the heart.

translation: Sleeplessness has made my eye its home
since the phantom of sleep forsook its lids.
8.sharh: The beloved's image no longer visits him in dreams, so he cannot sleep at all. Al-Lakhmi calls it the reverse of a line by Bashshar, where the visiting phantom is what keeps sleep away.

translation: then all I have met with can be forgiven
beside what the far road of parting has left of me.
9.sharh: This answers the “if” of line 2: grey hair and sleeplessness are nothing beside what exile has done. Al-Lakhmi takes what parting “has left” to be his own worn body; others, the memory of those he loves.

translation: If the solid rock had to bear a part
of what my heart endures, it would shatter the hardest stone.
10.sharh: What his heart bears would split solid rock. Al-Lakhmi puts the pain down to exile and separation from friends and home.

translation: When the fresh green branch begins to wilt, know
that all it can come to is wasting and ruin.
11.sharh: He is the branch: wilting now, and bound to dry up altogether. Al-Lakhmi notes that the verb means to wilt, not yet to wither completely.

translation: I choked; no, a choking gripped me
whose blocking is deadlier to me than any bone in the throat.
12.sharh: He corrects himself to make it worse: not a bone in the throat but a choking that could kill. Al-Lakhmi takes the choking to be the shame of asking others for favours, which lines 15 and 16 describe.

translation: If my endurance keeps my eye from weeping,
my heart is set on the paths of tears.
13.sharh: Dry eyes, a weeping heart: pride keeps his tears in, but inside he cries without end. Al-Lakhmi compares al-Abbas ibn al-Ahnaf: “My eye laughs while my heart weeps.”

translation: If dreams had whispered to me what I meet
awake, it would have struck me dead where I lay.
14.sharh: His waking life is worse than any nightmare: had he only dreamt what he lives through, the terror alone would have killed him. The verb is a hunter's word for a shot that kills on the spot.

translation: A plight I never thought that any man
of sense or understanding would accept for himself:
15.sharh: The next line says what this plight is: living in hope of other people's gifts. The commentators disagree on arab: al-Lakhmi glosses it as need, Ibn Khalawayh as intelligence.

translation: watching a cloud whose lightning brings no rain,
a standing between hoping and wishing.
16.sharh: This is the plight: waiting on patrons is like watching lightning that promises rain and never delivers, hanging between hope and wishful thinking.

translation: Each day a lodging that does not agree with me,
that drinks my lifeblood to the dregs, or one I loathe.
17.sharh: Every day another lodging: one that disagrees with his body though he likes it, or one his heart dislikes though it suits him. Al-Lakhmi and Ibn Khalawayh draw that distinction between the two words.

translation: I never thought Time would bend me down
to a hardship the lizard of the stony uplands would refuse.
18.sharh: He has sunk lower than he ever imagined: even the dabb, a desert lizard at home on bare rock, would not put up with his lot.

translation: I live on a trickle, just enough for breath, and if
I try to drink deep, I am reaching for what is hard to drink.
19.sharh: He gets barely enough to stay alive, like a man sipping at a trickle of water, and anything more, a real drink, is out of his reach.

translation: Will Time come back to me for a whole year
to what it used to give, or is there no hoping for it?
20.sharh: Will his luck ever return to what it was? Al-Lakhmi points out that he is not asking for a year of his past back, which is impossible, but for Time to treat him as it used to.

translation: Time, if you will not make amends, then go gently,
for your gentleness and your amends are the same to me.
21.sharh: If Time will not make up for the past, he will settle for being treated gently from now on; to him the two come to the same.

translation: Ease up on me; you have worn me down long enough.
Leave some sap in a branch already stripped of its bark.
22.sharh: He asks Time for a respite and to spare what life is left in him. Al-Lakhmi and Ibn Khalawayh read “you have worn me thin”; this recording has “you have tired me out”, a reading al-Lakhmi records.

translation: Do not think, Time, that I will grovel
before a disaster that strips me as knives strip a bone.
23.sharh: Having pleaded with Time, he turns defiant: whatever it does to him, even stripping him to the bone, he will not crawl before it.

translation: You have wrestled with a man who, if the heavens fell
on him from every side of the sky, would not complain.
24.sharh: He tells Time it has taken on a man who would not complain if the sky fell in on him. Ibn Khallikan reports that his pupil al-Qali privately thought the paralysis of the poet's last years a punishment for this line.

translation: But this is the spitting of a man sick in the chest:
when froth wells up on every side, it covers all.
25.sharh: He excuses his complaints: a man with a sick chest has to cough up what is there, as froth wells up round a camel's mouth. Al-Lakhmi and Ibn Khalawayh read “throws it off” for “covers”.

translation: I have accepted under compulsion, and under compulsion
accepts whoever resents the turns of fate.
26.sharh: He has accepted his lot only because he was forced to, and forced acceptance is all that anyone who resents the turns of fate can offer. He resigns himself to what he cannot change without pretending to like it.

translation: When the two ever-new ones take hold
of anything new, they bring it near to wearing out.
27.sharh: The “two new ones” are night and day, renewed for ever; whatever new thing they work on, here his body, they wear out. The play on “new” cannot be kept in English.

translation: I did not know (and Time loves
to scatter what is gathered and unpick strands that were spun)
28.sharh: The sentence runs on into the next line; in between he notes Time's habit of breaking up what holds together and unravelling what was firmly twisted.

translation: that fate would fling me into a pit
from which no one who falls in recovers.
29.sharh: He never knew fate had such a fall in store for him. Al-Lakhmi notes that the verb means to recover from illness, where “escape” would fit better.

translation: If, once my soul escapes this one, I stumble again,
then say, the two of you, “May he not rise.”
30.sharh: La'an was the wish for a man who stumbles: up you get. If he falls again after this lesson he deserves no such wish. Al-Lakhmi recalls “a believer is not stung twice from the same hole”.

translation: And if its length runs on until it meets
my death, I will set the comfort of example over grief.
31.sharh: If the disaster lasts until he dies, he will console himself with the example of greater men, and the next lines list them. Usa, examples, and asa, grief, differ only in their first vowel.

translation: Imru' al-Qays ran towards a goal,
and his death held him back short of it.
32.sharh: The first of his examples: the poet-prince Imru' al-Qays set out to win back his father's kingdom and died before he could. Al-Lakhmi and Ibn Khalawayh tell how the Byzantine emperor sent him a poisoned robe.

translation: A wasting sickness steeped the soul of Abu al-Jabr
until death gathered him among all it has gathered.
33.sharh: Abu al-Jabr, a king of Kinda, went to the Persian king for troops, and his own Persian escort poisoned him on the way home. The Arab physician al-Harith ibn Kalada cured him at Ta'if, but the sickness came back and killed him.

translation: Ibn al-Ashajj, the prince, drove himself to his death
rather than let his enemies gloat.
34.sharh: Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Ash'ath rebelled against al-Hajjaj and fled to Rutbil, a king beyond Sijistan. When Rutbil gave him up, he threw himself from a roof, still chained to his guard, sooner than give his enemies the pleasure.

translation: And the drawn sword of death cut al-Waddah off
before he reached what he had hoped for.
35.sharh: Al-Waddah is Jadhima al-Abrash, first king of al-Hira. Ignoring his adviser Qasir, he went to marry the queen al-Zabba', whose father he had killed, and she had him bled to death.

translation: Before me Yazid rose in pursuit
of the summit of glory, and neither flagged nor faltered,
36.sharh: Yazid ibn al-Muhallab, of the poet's own tribe of Azd, rose against the caliph Yazid ibn Abd al-Malik, took Basra and was killed fighting the caliph's brother Maslama. The next line finishes his story.

translation: And there rose up, short of what he sought, when things had turned grim,
the all-devouring, overwhelming disaster.
37.sharh: Yazid's story ends: disaster came between him and his goal, which al-Lakhmi says was the caliphate itself. Luhaym and uraba are two of the many Arabic names for calamity.

translation: Am I the first of noble chiefs
whom the turns of Time have wronged and assailed?
38.sharh: A question that expects the answer no: he is not the first great man brought down by fortune, so he can bear it. Al-Lakhmi compares Qays ibn al-Khatim's “I am not the first man struck by disaster.”

translation: If fate grants me what I am striving for,
I will spare no pains to mend the breach.
39.sharh: If fortune ever lets him reach his aim, he will use it to heal what has been broken among his people; tha'a is a rift or damage that needs mending.

translation: Amr rose up to avenge his blood-debts
and brought down from them all that stood highest.
40.sharh: Amr ibn Adi, Jadhima's nephew and heir, took revenge for him, and the highest of his targets was the queen al-Zabba' herself. After men cut off short of their goals come men who reached them.

translation: He forced al-Zabba' down, though she was set
higher than an eagle in the open sky.
41.sharh: Al-Zabba' seemed out of reach, but Amr's adviser Qasir smuggled armed men into her city in sacks on camelback. She took poison rather than die at Amr's hand: “By my own hand, not Amr's.”

translation: And Sayf, whose resolve raised him high
until he cast himself at the farthest of all marks:
42.sharh: Sayf ibn Dhi Yazan, a prince of Himyar, went to the Persian king for help against the Abyssinians who had taken Yemen. The army he brought back, under the old general Wahriz, drove them out.

translation: he made the Abyssinians gulp deadly poison
and took his seat in Ghumdan's chamber of images.
43.sharh: He destroyed the Abyssinians and enthroned himself in Ghumdan, the great palace of San'a. Al-Lakhmi and Ibn Khalawayh quote Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt's praise of him there: “Drink in health, the crown upon you.”

translation: Then Ibn Hind, whose fires laid hold
of Tamim with burning on the Day of Uwarat.
44.sharh: Amr ibn Hind, king of al-Hira, swore to burn a hundred men of Tamim to avenge his brother. He burned ninety-nine; a traveller who came looking for the roast made up the hundred, and became the proverb “the unlucky one is the traveller of al-Barajim”.

translation: Whenever despair came whispering to my resolve,
hope rose to challenge it, and it hid away.
45.sharh: After the examples, the point: despair never wins with him, for hope always faces it down. Al-Lakhmi sets it against a line of Ibrahim ibn al-Abbas al-Suli, where despair is sent against greed.

translation: I swear by the hardy she-camels that speed
flings onward through the heart of the wastes,
46.sharh: A long oath begins, by the camels carrying pilgrims to Mecca; it is broken off and taken up again, and its answer comes only in line 72. Swearing by the pilgrims' camels was a convention of Arabic verse.

translation: hollow-eyed, like the frames of bent bows, and lean,
their noses running blood and slime from the tug of the nose-rings,
47.sharh: The camels are worn to skin and bone by the journey, as thin and curved as bows; the constant pull of the nose-rings has made their noses bleed.

translation: They sink by night into a sea of darkness, and by forenoon
they float on the mirage when the mirage rises.
48.sharh: By night the camels vanish into the dark as if sinking into the sea; by day they seem to float on the shimmering mirage. Abd al-Qahir al-Jurjani quotes the line in his Secrets of Eloquence.

translation: Their pads, from wear and soreness,
are split, and dye the white pebbles red.
49.sharh: The camels' feet are so worn by the stony road that they leave blood on the white pebbles: the hardship of the pilgrimage told through the animals.

translation: They carry every pilgrim, sallow and bent double
from the endless toil of dawn starts and night marches,
50.sharh: The riders are as worn as their mounts, pale and bowed by the endless round of early starts and night journeys on the road to Mecca.

translation: devout, his body pared away by long hunger,
so that he is like an arrow-shaft of nab' wood, bent in the back.
51.sharh: The pilgrim is devout, and long hunger has pared him down to an arrow-shaft of nab', thin and hard, his back bowed by the road. Nab' was the hard mountain wood used for the best bows and arrows.

translation: He heads for the town the Lord on high preferred
above all dwellings when He spread out its earth.
52.sharh: The pilgrim makes for Mecca. Al-Lakhmi says the line versifies the tradition that God spread out the earth from beneath Mecca, which is why it is called the Mother of Cities.

translation: Until, when he comes face to face with it, his tears well up:
he cannot hold back his eyes' tears where they flow.
53.sharh: The pilgrim weeps at his first sight of Mecca. Al-Lakhmi traces the first half to Majnun Layla, who burst into tears at the sight of Mount Tawbadh.

translation: Then he circled the House and turned to touch the Stone,
then came to the two hills, and walked between them.
54.sharh: The rites in order: the circuits of the Ka'ba, touching the Black Stone, then the walk between the hills of al-Safa and al-Marwa, here called “the two Marwas”.

translation: He bound himself to the hajj and joined an umra to it,
after crying out, answering the call and praying.
55.sharh: He performs hajj and umra together, after crying out the pilgrim's “Here I am, O God”. Al-Lakhmi recalls the Prophet's description of the best hajj: “crying out and the flowing of sacrificial blood”.

translation: Then at evening he set off among the pilgrims crying “Here I am”
for where the two Ma'zims rise, and Mina.
56.sharh: He moves on with the crowd of pilgrims towards Mina and the two Ma'zims, the hills that close the way between Muzdalifa and Arafat.

translation: Then he came to Arafat, going humbly
from station to station between Alal and the dune.
57.sharh: The day of standing at Arafat, the heart of the hajj, moving from one place of prayer to the next. Alal is the hill at Arafat where the imam stands.

translation: He began the seven afresh, and seven after them,
and the seven run between the slopes and the cairns.
58.sharh: Al-Lakhmi takes this as the seven circuits of the Ka'ba and the seven walks between al-Safa and al-Marwa; others read it as the stoning, seven pebbles at each pillar.

translation: And at evening he went with the others to bid the House farewell,
his reward secured, shunning foul and idle talk.
59.sharh: The pilgrimage ends with the farewell circuit; the pilgrim has earned his reward and kept clear of the obscene and frivolous talk the hajj forbids.

translation: By that do I swear, or by horses running at full stretch,
their withers high and their flanks drawn lean,
60.sharh: Having sworn by the pilgrims' camels, he wonders whether to swear instead by war-horses. Al-Lakhmi reads the “or” as a real choice, Ibn Khalawayh as “nay, rather”.

translation: shaggy-maned, racing like the wolves of the ghada,
eyes askance, keeping pace with the spear-points,
61.sharh: Wild-maned horses race like wolves, eyeing sideways in pride, their long necks holding their heads level with the spear-tips. Al-Lakhmi says most transmissions lack this line.

translation: carrying every keen, fearsome warrior,
sharp of heart, who wades into the thick of battle.
62.sharh: The riders match their horses: tensed for combat and quick of heart, they plunge into the deepest part of the fight as into deep water.

translation: He meets war's fire with his cheeks to the flame
when the blaze of war is hateful to come near.
63.sharh: He faces the battle head on, when others shrink from its heat. Al-Lakhmi and Ibn Khalawayh read “the fire of death” for “the fire of war”.

translation: If death were given shape before him as a foe,
no awe would turn him from it, nor would he give ground.
64.sharh: Even if Death itself took shape and stood before him as an opponent in single combat, the man would neither hesitate nor turn away.

translation: Were Fate to shield a life from him,
he would go after it until he had made free with what Fate shielded.
65.sharh: He is a rival to Fate itself: what Fate protects, he pursues until he takes it. Al-Lakhmi calls him Fate's partner in men's lives.

translation: The deaths go out each morning at his bidding:
they will what he wills and refuse what he refuses.
66.sharh: Death itself takes his orders in battle. Al-Lakhmi compares Abu al-Atahiya: “as if death ran in battle only at your command”.

translation: Nay, rather an oath by the proud lords of Ya'rub: is there,
for one who swears, any further to go after this?
67.sharh: He breaks off and swears by something greater still, the nobles of Ya'rub, ancestor of the southern Arabs and of the poet's own tribe. After that oath there is nothing left to swear by.

translation: They are those who, when they vie for glory, make glory say:
“Dust in the mouth of any man who vies with you.”
68.sharh: So great are they that glory itself curses their rivals; “dust in his mouth” is the Arabic way of wishing a man failure. Al-Lakhmi finds the phrase in al-Farazdaq.

translation: They are those who set the springs of bounty flowing,
pouring for all who came to them and asked.
69.sharh: Their generosity runs like springwater for anyone who comes asking. Arabic has two verbs here for coming in search of a gift, both used of guests and suppliants.

translation: They are those who humbled whoever swelled with pride
and set straight the haughty cheek and whoever leaned aside.
70.sharh: They put down the arrogant and straightened the crooked. Sa'ar, the proud tilt of the cheek, is the word of the Quran's “Do not turn your cheek away from people in pride.”

translation: They are those who made their adversaries swallow
the milk of humiliation, draught on bitter draught.
71.sharh: Their enemies are made to drink humiliation again and again, like milk that gathers in the udder between milkings and is drawn off once more, every draught of it bitter. Their shame is renewed whenever it seems to be over.

translation: I shall go on wearing a close-woven coat of mail
until I am hidden among the heaped earth of the grave.
72.sharh: Here at last is what the long oath swears to: he will never take off his armour until he is buried. The negative is left out of “I shall not cease”, as Arabic allows after an oath.

translation: My two companions: a cutting sword, along whose back
runs something like the track of ants climbing hillocks,
73.sharh: His two companions are his sword and his horse. The watered pattern of a fine blade, the wavy grain in the steel, looks like the trail of ants over little hills. The horse comes in line 78.

translation: white as salt when you draw it,
its edge meets nothing that it does not cut through.
74.sharh: The sword gleams white and cuts whatever it touches. Al-Lakhmi says this line is missing from most transmissions, and Ibn Khalawayh does not have it.

translation: As if between its midrib and its edge
were an oven where live coals devour each other.
75.sharh: The flicker of light along the blade, from the raised spine to the edge, is like coals glowing and eating into each other in a bread oven.

translation: It shows Death, as Death follows its track,
paths through the darkness of livers that no eye can see.
76.sharh: The sword is death's guide, opening hidden ways into the body for death to follow. Al-Lakhmi compares Abu Tammam, who makes parting the guide of death.

translation: When it falls on a body it leaves it,
even, where before it had been odd.
77.sharh: One stroke cuts a man in two. Khasa and zaka are old words for odd and even, used in a guessing game; Ibn Khalawayh uses them to explain the Quran's “the even and the odd”.

translation: and a horse high in all its points, packed with firm flesh,
its last ribs well sprung, broad-chested, tight in the thigh-vein,
78.sharh: The second companion: a tall, solid horse. Each phrase names a point the Arab horseman looked for, from the high croup and withers to the hard flesh and the taut sinew down the thigh.

translation: short between croup and back,
long between the nape and the root of the tail,
79.sharh: A compact back on a long body. Al-Lakhmi lists such pairs, near and far, among the fourteen points of a good horse, and quotes another maqsura that counts them.

translation: high-necked, rising from a full base,
broad in the breast, on sinews that will not let him stumble,
80.sharh: A high neck set on a deep base, a wide chest, and strong legs that can be trusted not to trip.

translation: set in pasterns well covered,
down to hoof-frogs like spat-out date stones.
81.sharh: His legs end in well-fleshed pasterns and hooves whose undersides are as hard as date stones, the hardest thing a desert Arab knew.

translation: He crushes the pebbles on the open plains, and if he climbs
to the hills he strikes from them the fire of the fireflies.
82.sharh: His hooves smash stones on the flat and strike sparks on rocky ground. Nar al-hubahib, the spark-fire, was the proverbial fire that warms no one.

translation: He turns two ears like seed-pods on a compact head,
with two flashing eyes that glance like a wild ox.
83.sharh: Small, pricked ears, likened to the slender pods of the markh shrub, a round, compact head and keen, wide eyes like those of the wild ox: all marks of a thoroughbred.

translation: compact of build, wide between the jaws,
smooth where the rider sits, twisted hard like rope, strong.
84.sharh: More points of the horse: a compact, tightly knit body, a wide space between the jaws, a smooth back where the rider sits, and muscles twisted hard like a well-made rope.

translation: No knocking hocks disfigure him, no splayed legs,
no swelling to weaken his hoof, no splint on his foreleg.
85.sharh: He is free of every fault a horse-dealer looks for: the hocks do not knock, the legs do not splay, the hooves are sound and the forelegs clean.

translation: If you struck out across the whole earth on his back,
riding it end to end, you would not fear he would go lame.
86.sharh: You could ride him across the world off the roads and he would never go footsore. Al-Lakhmi says most transmissions lack this line.

translation: He runs, and the wind stumbles in his course
and falls back spent, taking shelter in the roots of the shrubs.
87.sharh: He is faster than the wind, which tries to keep up and drops exhausted behind him. Al-Lakhmi traces the image to Muslim ibn al-Walid.

translation: You would think, though he is in plain sight, that he was hidden
from every eye, whether he gallops or canters.
88.sharh: He moves so fast that, though you are looking straight at him, he seems invisible. The two verbs name two of the Arab horse's gaits.

translation: If you strain your eyes along his track,
you would say: a flash of light, or lightning glinting.
89.sharh: All you see is a flash, like lightning. Khafa can mean both to hide and to appear; here it is the glint of lightning.

translation: It is as if Gemini were in his pasterns
and the Pleiades on his brow when he comes in sight.
90.sharh: The horse's white markings shine like stars: his white stockings are the stars of Gemini at his feet, and the blaze on his forehead is the Pleiades. Both marks were prized in a thoroughbred.

translation: These two are my gear, enough to make up for the loss
of anyone I counted on; let him go who wants to go.
91.sharh: His sword and his horse are all the gear he needs: with them he can do without anyone he once relied on, and friends who want to leave him are free to go.

translation: If you hear of a millstone set up
for war, know that I am the pivot of that mill.
92.sharh: War is a turning millstone, and he is its pivot: the man the fighting turns on. The image of war as a mill is an old one in Arabic poetry.

translation: And if you see a fire of war blazing,
know that I am the one who stoked that blaze.
93.sharh: Wherever war flares up, he is the one who lit it; a mis'ar, a stoker of war, was praise for a brave man.

translation: The best of lives are those that pour out in the open
on the edges of whetted swords and spears.
94.sharh: The noblest death is to fall in battle. Nafs is both soul and blood, so a life “pours out”. Al-Lakhmi traces the line to al-Samaw'al: “Our lives pour out on the edges of blades.”

translation: Iraq: I did not leave its people
out of hatred that turned me away, or for any loathing.
95.sharh: He left his homeland, Iraq, for Fars, but not because he disliked its people. Al-Lakhmi compares Ishaq al-Mawsili leaving Baghdad “not out of loathing”.

translation: Nor since I left them has anything drawn my eyes
that pleases the sight, among all the people there are.
96.sharh: Since leaving Iraq he has found no one to admire. Al-Lakhmi compares Imran ibn Hittan's lament for Mirdas: “People are not people since you went.”

translation: They are mountain peaks, their summits towering;
other people, beside them, are potholes and pits.
97.sharh: His people in Iraq are towering mountain peaks; everyone else, set beside them, is a pothole or a pit in the ground.

translation: They are seas with surging waves;
other people are shallows, rock pools and puddles.
98.sharh: The same contrast in water: they are deep seas, others are the shallow water a man wades through, or rainwater caught in a hollow of rock.

translation: If I have seen, since I left them, their equal,
then may I shut my eyes on the prick of thorns.
99.sharh: An oath in the form of a curse on himself: if he has seen their like, may thorns pierce his eyes. The next line makes an exception.

translation: Except the two emirs who sent
to me a shade of ease that spread wide.
100.sharh: Except for his patrons, the two Mikali emirs of Fars. Al-Mas'udi, quoted by Ibn Khallikan, names them as Abd Allah ibn Muhammad ibn Mikal and his son Abu al-Abbas; al-Lakhmi, from al-Qali, makes them brothers.

translation: They are the two who set firm for me a hope
that despair had left standing on the brink.
101.sharh: His hope stood on the edge of a cliff, about to be pushed over by despair, when the two emirs pulled it back and set it on firm ground.

translation: They mended a life that the turns of Time
had muddied, and it went down sweet again, and clear.
102.sharh: Life is a drink that Time had stirred up into mud; the emirs made it clear and easy to swallow again.

translation: They set the water of plenty flowing for me,
and my branch stirred and grew after it had withered.
103.sharh: Their gifts were rain on dry ground: his withered branch, an echo of line 11, came back to life. Al-Lakhmi and Ibn Khalawayh cite the Quran on rain making dead earth stir and swell.

translation: They are the two who lifted up my gaze
after I had lowered my eyes on the smart of motes.
104.sharh: Want and humiliation had kept his eyes down, smarting as if specks were in them; the emirs let him hold his head up.

translation: They are the two who rebuilt for me a quarter
of hope that had long since fallen to ruin.
105.sharh: The two emirs revived a hope he had long given up. Hope is pictured as a house that had stood in ruins for years, and their gifts rebuilt one part of it so that it could be lived in again.

translation: They hung on my neck a favour that, if the thanks
of all the people of the earth were set against it for me, would not match
106.sharh: He wears their kindness like a necklace; all mankind's thanks, offered on his behalf, would not repay it. The sentence runs on into the next line.

translation: a tenth of a tenth of it, and it would be
like a sip of water in the waves of a sea at flood.
107.sharh: All the world's thanks would not come to one part in a hundred of what he owes them: a mouthful against the ocean.

translation: Ibn Mikal, the emir, drew me up
after I had been like a thing tossed aside.
108.sharh: The patron is named: Ibn Mikal raised him from nothing. Ibn Khalawayh says Ibn Durayd wrote both his great dictionary, al-Jamhara, and this poem for him.

translation: And Abu al-Abbas lifted me by the arms
after my strength had shrunk and my reach had grown short.
109.sharh: The second patron, Abu al-Abbas, raised him when poverty had left him powerless. A narrow “arm's span” is the Arabic idiom for helplessness, still used today.

translation: He is the one who kept on rising towards the heights
by his deeds, until he rose above the heights.
110.sharh: He did not stop at the summit of glory but went beyond it. Al-Lakhmi says this line and the next are missing from most transmissions.

translation: If anyone could climb by his generosity
and his glory to the sky, he would have climbed.
111.sharh: Praise by hyperbole: if virtue could lift a man to heaven, his patron would be there. Al-Lakhmi traces it to a line often credited to Zuhayr.

translation: No seeker of favours ever came to the sea of his bounty
burning with craving, without going away quenched.
112.sharh: No one who came to him in need went away unsatisfied. Al-Lakhmi's editor notes that one of his manuscripts lacks this line and another marks it as doubtful.

translation: My soul is a ransom for my two emirs, and whoever
lives under the sky is a ransom for my two emirs.
113.sharh: He would give his life, and everyone else's, for the two emirs. The word for ransom appears twice, once long and once short.

translation: May my thanks to them stay joined
to my words, until the turn of fate holds me back.
114.sharh: He will thank them for as long as he lives: their praise will be on his tongue until death stops it.

translation: Those I left, not out of hatred:
my heart has not turned from them, nor wavered.
115.sharh: He returns to the friends he left behind in Iraq: he did not leave them out of dislike, and distance has not turned his heart from them or made it waver.

translation: But I have a resolve that, when I ride it
at a closed and baffling affair, splits it, and it breaks open.
116.sharh: He left them not for lack of love but because his resolve drives him on: ridden like a mount against any knotted problem, it splits it open.

translation: Had I wished, youth would have spread its two wings
over me in a shade of comfort and wealth,
117.sharh: Had he wanted, he could have stayed young at heart and lived in ease and plenty; he chose to leave instead. The next lines describe the pleasures he passed up.

translation: and a soft and languid girl would have dallied with me,
who wastes a man with sickness, though the cure is in her kiss.
118.sharh: Had he wished, a soft, languid girl would have played with him: she wastes her lovers with longing, and the only cure is to kiss her. The beloved who is both sickness and cure is a commonplace of Arabic love poetry.

translation: If she gives you a look of anger,
her glance is a sword that cuts through your inmost parts.
119.sharh: Her angry glance is a sword that cuts through a man's insides: the look kills as a blade does. Al-Lakhmi says this line and the next are missing from most transmissions.

translation: In her cheek there is a garden of roses over
eglantine, and its flowers are picked by glances.
120.sharh: Her cheeks are red roses laid over white eglantine, the mingled red and white prized in a beautiful face. It is a garden no hand may touch: only eyes can pick its flowers.

translation: If she whispered to the mountain goat, it would come down to her,
led on a halter, from the high crags of the peaks.
121.sharh: Her voice would charm the wariest of creatures, the ibex that keeps to the cliff-tops, and bring it down to her as tame as a led animal.

translation: Or if she came upon a hermit at prayer on a smooth peak,
hard of access and rough to climb,
122.sharh: Even a holy man who has withdrawn to an inaccessible mountain would not be safe; the sentence runs on into the next line.

translation: her company would turn him from his prayers and his faith
until you saw him turned a love-struck boy.
123.sharh: Her company would draw the hermit from his prayers and his faith until he was a lovesick youth again. Al-Lakhmi traces the hermit to al-Nabigha, whose grey-haired monk would gaze at the beloved and think himself rightly guided.

translation: As if wine were mixed into it
with the water of fresh-picked roses, when the night grows dark,
124.sharh: Her kisses taste of wine mixed with rosewater, and the sentence runs on into the next line. Her breath at night is a stock test of a woman's sweetness.

translation: which the one who sips the coolness of her mouth draws up
between the gleam of her teeth and the dark of her lips.
125.sharh: The lover drinks from her mouth as from a well, between white teeth and dark lips; Arabs prized a darkish tint in the lips.

translation: May it water al-Aqiq, and al-Haziz, and al-Mala,
and on to al-Nahit and the near villages,
126.sharh: A prayer for rain over the places of his youth near Basra, the traditional blessing on a beloved landscape. What brings the rain, a dark cloud, comes only in line 131.

translation: and the Upper Mirbad, where you will find
lions laid low by the glances of wild cows,
127.sharh: The Mirbad, Basra's great market and gathering place, where brave men fall to the glances of beautiful women. Lions and wild cows are the stock images of men and women.

translation: the home of every noble chief whom
the deeds of his fathers raised to the top of the branch of glory,
128.sharh: The places he prays for are the home of Basra's noblemen, men whose fathers' great deeds have lifted them to the top of the tree of glory.

translation: of those whose stock, when they trace their descent,
is of the stock from which came the chosen Prophet,
129.sharh: The people of al-Mirbad, when they name their ancestors, come from the same stock as the Prophet: they are Arabs of the noblest descent. Neither al-Lakhmi nor Ibn Khalawayh says which clans he means.

translation: God bless him as long as darkness falls
and the morning sun runs in its sphere.
130.sharh: He breaks off to bless the Prophet, named in the line before, for as long as night falls and the sun runs its course. Ibn Khalawayh's text lacks it.

translation: a dark cloud to which the south wind lent
one of its flanks, and whose rain the hand of the east wind kept up.
131.sharh: The rain-cloud, the subject of the prayer in line 126, arrives: dark and heavy, pushed by the south wind and fed by the east, the two rain-bringing winds.

translation: It rose far off in the south, and when
its flanks spread out and its lower hems stretched wide, it covered all.
132.sharh: The cloud builds up far off in the south, then spreads out like a vast tent whose lower hems are let down on every side, until it covers everything beneath it.

translation: It cloaked the horizon, so that on every side
it seemed the white clouds came crawling in from its edges,
133.sharh: The cloud fills the whole horizon; on every side more white clouds seem to come crawling in from its edges to join it, so that no gap of open sky is left.

translation: and it covered the earth, so that every patch of it
would say: “It is here that the rain has come to stay.”
134.sharh: The rain falls so evenly that every patch of ground thinks it is the favoured one. Al-Lakhmi traces the image to Imru' al-Qays.

translation: Whenever its lightnings died down, the east wind
came upon them and fanned up whatever had died down.
135.sharh: Whenever the cloud's lightning dies down, the east wind blows on it and lights it again: lightning is fire, and the wind is the bellows that keeps it burning.

translation: And if its thunders slackened, the south wind,
a camel-driver, sang them on, and they sang as he sang.
136.sharh: The south wind drives the thunder like a camel-driver who sings to keep his herd moving, and the thunder answers in song.

translation: As if in its flanks and in its breast
there were couched camels calling to each other, moaning and lowing.
137.sharh: Thunder rolls through the cloud like the noise of a herd of kneeling camels groaning and calling to one another: the cloud is so full of it that it seems a whole camp of beasts.

translation: I never saw the like of the clouds: grazing herds left loose,
you would think them tended, though they roam untended.
138.sharh: Clouds are like a herd grazing with no herdsman: they move across the sky in such order that you would think someone drove them, yet only the winds do.

translation: It said to the parched lands, when they had gathered
all it drove to them: “Rest assured of water and green.”
139.sharh: Once it has gathered over them, the cloud tells the parched stretches of land to rest assured: water and fresh grazing are on their way.

translation: It flooded the rises with a gift that was more than enough,
and brimmed the hollows with plentiful water.
140.sharh: The rain gives the high ground more than enough and fills the hollows to the brim: no rise and no low place is left out.

translation: After its downpour the desert looked
like a sea whose current swelled and then lay calm.
141.sharh: The flooded desert becomes a sea, first heaving, then still. Al-Lakhmi traces it to al-Sadusi and thought al-Mutanabbi's version of the image fuller.

translation: May that rain be kept always for a people
who are themselves rain and bounty to the earth.
142.sharh: The prayer for rain ends in praise: may such rain be kept for a people who are themselves rain and bounty to the land, as generous as the rain itself.

translation: I am not, when a flood of trouble weighs me down,
one to say: “The torrent has reached the lion-pits.”
143.sharh: He never says things have gone too far. Pits for trapping lions were dug on high ground, so a flood that reached them had passed every limit; Ibn Khalawayh says the caliph Uthman used the phrase when besieged.

translation: And if a sigh lodges under my ribs
that fills me from one side to the other,
144.sharh: If a sigh of grief or anger lodges under his ribs and fills his chest from side to side, as water fills a well to its rim, the next line tells what he does with it.

translation: I check it, holding it down, until what had risen
in a flood is seen brought low.
145.sharh: He masters his grief or anger: the sigh of the line before is pressed back until it lies quiet. Ibn Khalawayh links it to the Quran's praise of “those who restrain their anger”.

translation: Nor, when a disaster strikes me, do I say
as the hopeless say: “The caul has split in the belly.”
146.sharh: He never talks like a man who has given up. The proverb he refuses to use is said of a case past saving: when the birth sac tears inside the she-camel, the young dies.

translation: Disasters have wrestled in me a hardened man
who grapples with terror when terror rises high.
147.sharh: Misfortunes have tried him again and again and found a tough, seasoned man, one who goes out to meet danger at its height instead of running from it.

translation: I am crooked if my enemy turns crooked,
and straight if my friend is straight.
148.sharh: He pays everyone back in kind, twisted with the twisted and straight with the straight. The two halves answer each other word for word: crooked against straight, enemy against friend.

translation: To my enemy I taste at times of colocynth,
to whoever seeks my love, of honey mixed with wine.
149.sharh: He is bitter to enemies and sweet to friends. Colocynth is the proverbially bitter gourd of the desert; honey mixed with wine is the sweetest drink he can name.

translation: Pliant when I am handled gently, easy to bend,
stubborn when handled roughly, and my sting is feared.
150.sharh: Gentle with those who are gentle, hard and dangerous with those who are rough. Ibn Khalawayh compares the Quran's “humble towards the believers, mighty against the unbelievers”.

translation: My forbearance clings to both sides of my hibwa
when the winds of folly blow men's hibwas away.
151.sharh: He keeps his composure when others lose theirs. A man who leapt up in anger undid the cloth he sat wrapped in, so a hibwa blown loose means a temper lost.

translation: No soiling greed can lure me
when greed sways other men and draws them in.
152.sharh: He cannot be bought. Greed tempts others into what stains their name, but not him. Al-Lakhmi and Ibn Khalawayh quote Thabit Qutna: “No good in a greed that leads to disgrace.”

translation: My trials have raised me through rank after rank
and set me overlooking the paths of reason.
153.sharh: Experience has lifted him step by step to a height from which he can see where wisdom leads, as a man on a ridge sees the roads below.

translation: When another man is feared for the harm he heaps on men,
no rashness is feared from me, and no harm.
154.sharh: Where others are dreaded for their violence, nobody need fear his temper or his hand. The next line explains why he holds back.

translation: Not from any weakness: I am a man
who guards an honour that no stain has clouded.
155.sharh: His restraint is not weakness but care for his good name, which he keeps unclouded. Al-Lakhmi traces it to Hassan ibn Thabit: “I guard my honour with my wealth.”

translation: A man guards his honour by giving away
what is held too dear, of all he has gathered and picked out.
156.sharh: The way to keep one's honour is to spend one's best possessions freely: wealth is there to protect a name, not the other way round.

translation: Praise is the best shield that you can take up,
and after piety, the most precious thing laid by.
157.sharh: A good name protects a man better than armour, and only piety is worth more as a treasure. Al-Lakhmi finds the second half in a line of al-Akhtal on good deeds as the best savings.

translation: Every generation that springs up in an age
resembles the age in which it appeared.
158.sharh: People take after their times. Al-Lakhmi says this puts into verse a saying of Umar ibn al-Khattab: “People resemble their age more than they resemble their fathers.”

translation: People are like plants: some look lovely,
fresh and bright of stem, and bitter in their fruit.
159.sharh: Looks deceive: some people are handsome and fresh but bitter once you come to know them, like a green plant whose fruit is gall.

translation: And some the eye passes over, but if you taste
their fruit, it goes down sweet and easy in the throat.
160.sharh: The opposite case: plain-looking people who prove sweet and good once known. Al-Lakhmi notes that he leaves out those good inside and out, and those bad in both.

translation: A youth can be straightened from his crookedness,
and what was bent and bowed in him stands true.
161.sharh: The young can still be corrected. This line and the next two set the young man, the old man and the green branch side by side.

translation: But the old man, if you try to straighten him,
no truing will right what has grown bent in him.
162.sharh: The old cannot change: their faults have set hard. Al-Lakhmi traces these lines to Sabiq al-Barbari: “Branches come true when you straighten them; dry timber will not bend.”

translation: So too the branch: easy to bend
while it is supple, hard to press once it has hardened.
163.sharh: Like a youth, a green branch bends easily while it is supple, but once it has dried and hardened no pressure will bend it. The image sums up the two lines before.

translation: Whoever wrongs people, they steer clear of his wrong,
and both his flanks are strong and guarded among them.
164.sharh: A bitter observation: people respect those who can hurt them. Al-Lakhmi traces it to Zuhayr: “Whoever does not wrong people is wronged.”

translation: But to the man who is gentle with them
they are crueller than the snakes in the spoil of wells.
165.sharh: The gentle get no mercy. “More unjust than a snake” is a proverb: the snake takes over burrows other creatures have dug.

translation: And people, all of them, if you search them out
through every region of the lands and villages,
166.sharh: The sentence runs on into the next line. This line is missing from Ibn Khalawayh's text and from one of al-Lakhmi's manuscripts.

translation: are slaves of the man of wealth, though they hope
not even for a mouthful of his plenty to ease their thirst.
167.sharh: People fawn on the rich even when they expect nothing from them. Al-Lakhmi cites a similar complaint by the pre-Islamic poet Aws ibn Hajar.

translation: And they are enemies to the man who falls poor,
though he once shared with them all he gained and owned.
168.sharh: Past generosity earns the poor man nothing. Al-Lakhmi compares Urwa ibn al-Ward: “I have seen that the worst of men, in people's eyes, is the poor.”

translation: I have bitten into my days; the green youth is not
like the man round whom Time has wrapped itself as waist-cloth and mantle.
169.sharh: He has tested life the way one bites a stick to try its hardness. An untried youth is no match for a man whom Time has wrapped round, through every turn of fortune.

translation: Wit is no use without luck,
and ignorance will not bring you low when luck is high.
170.sharh: Fortune counts for more than brains. Jadd, luck, is the word in the Prophet's prayer “the fortune of the fortunate avails nothing against You”.

translation: Whoever is not taught by Time will gain nothing
from what a preacher brings him, at evening or at dawn.
171.sharh: If life itself has taught a man nothing, no preacher will, whether he comes at nightfall or at daybreak. The lesson has to come from within.

translation: Whoever draws no lessons from his days,
blindness suits him better than guidance.
172.sharh: A man who learns nothing from what he has lived through has eyes to no purpose; he might as well be blind.

translation: Whoever measures what he has not seen by what he has,
the near will show him the far.
173.sharh: Experience is a guide to the unknown: whoever judges what he has not seen by what he has, finds the far brought near and made plain.

translation: Whoever hands his halter to greed will go on
lapping at the stale water of humiliation.
174.sharh: Greed is a master that leads its slave by the halter to drink, head down, from a pool gone stale: the humiliation of always wanting more.

translation: Whoever meets his cravings with renunciation,
the eye of honour turns to him wherever he looks.
175.sharh: Dignity comes from wanting nothing from others. Renounce your cravings and honour itself will look your way, in whatever direction you look.

translation: Whoever bends his soul to what it dislikes,
wealth is his companion wherever he sets out.
176.sharh: Self-denial makes a man rich, because contentment travels with him. Ibn Khalawayh quotes the Prophet's saying “Wealth is not many possessions; wealth is a rich soul.”

translation: Whoever does not stop at the limit of his worth,
even the widest strides fall short for him.
177.sharh: A man who will not stop at the limit of his worth never arrives: however wide his strides, they fall short. Al-Lakhmi sets it beside al-Mutanabbi's “Whoever's soul does not know its worth”.

translation: Whoever throws prudence away reaps for himself
a regret that burns worse than the scorch of fire.
178.sharh: Carelessness breeds remorse that burns worse than fire. Al-Lakhmi traces it to two lines in which Amr ibn al-As reproaches Mu'awiya: “I gave you a prudent order and you disobeyed me.”

translation: Whoever ties the loops of his character to conceit,
the loops of loathing are tied to those same loops.
179.sharh: Vanity draws hatred as surely as one loop is knotted to another. The image is of the loops on a bucket or a garment, fastened together.

translation: Whoever reaches beyond the limit of his reach
fails to win the near, let alone the far.
180.sharh: Whoever grasps at more than his reach loses even what was within it, never mind what lay beyond: the same lesson as the line before, that overreaching ends in failure.

translation: Whoever tries to carry what is past his strength
of a load, one day ends up with his back broken.
181.sharh: Overreaching again, in the image of a beast under too heavy a load: whoever takes on more than he can bear ends with a broken back. Al-Lakhmi calls it the opposite of Amr ibn Ma'dikarib's “If you cannot do a thing, leave it.”

translation: People: a thousand of them may count as one,
and one may count as a thousand when trouble comes.
182.sharh: Men are not equal: a crowd can be worth less than one man of mettle. Ibn Khalawayh tells how the caliph Umar, sending four men to Egypt, wrote that he was sending four thousand.

translation: A man owns of his wealth what his hands
sent on ahead before he died, not what he hoarded.
183.sharh: Only what is spent or given away in a lifetime truly belongs to a man. Al-Lakhmi traces the line to the hadith: “Yours is only what you ate and used up, wore and wore out, or gave away and sent on.”

translation: A man is only a story after he is gone,
so be a good story for whoever remembers.
184.sharh: After death all that is left of a man is what people say of him; live so that the story is worth telling.

translation: I have milked Time from both its halves:
at times it has been bitter to me, and at times sweet.
185.sharh: He has known both the good and the bad of life. “Milking Time from both halves” comes from milking first the front teats of a she-camel, then the back.

translation: My tooth has laid bare my trials; so speak of me
as of a grown camel that has broken in hardships and ridden them.
186.sharh: His teeth tell his age and his trials, as a beast's teeth do when its lips are parted. The bazil is a camel in its prime, nine years old, strong enough for anything.

translation: People are green fodder for death, which crops them,
and fresh fodder seldom lasts under the cropping.
187.sharh: Death grazes on mankind as a beast crops fresh grass, nibbling it down blade by blade; grass seldom survives the grazing, and in the end no one is spared.

translation: I wonder at one who is sure that death,
when it comes for him, cannot be cured with charms,
188.sharh: He marvels at men who know death is beyond any cure, yet live as if it were not coming; the next line finishes the thought.

translation: yet lies in a deep pit of heedlessness,
like one beating trees for leaves between darkness and failing sight.
189.sharh: Such a man gropes about like someone knocking down leaves for his camels in the dark: he cannot see what he is doing, and Ibn Khalawayh adds that he may strike a snake.

translation: We are (with no ingratitude to God) like
what was said of the one out at pasture: “He found fresh fodder, and grazed.”
190.sharh: People are like a beast that has wandered into good pasture and thinks of nothing but eating. The aside, “with no ingratitude to God”, shows he is not complaining of God's gifts, only of how people forget themselves in them.

translation: When it hears a faint sound it takes fright, and when
the sound dies away it goes back to its play.
191.sharh: A grazing beast starts at a faint sound and goes back to its play once it fades. Ibn Khalawayh draws the moral: we are shaken for an hour when we see a funeral, then return to our amusements.

translation: like a flock that took fright at a lion and huddled,
until, when it was out of sight, it settled because it had gone.
192.sharh: The same picture again: sheep huddle while the lion is near and forget him once he is gone. Al-Lakhmi says this line is missing from most transmissions, and that these lines come from Salih ibn Abd al-Quddus: “We take fright when funerals pass us.”

translation: We take fright at whatever alarms us,
and once it has passed we graze on in heedlessness.
193.sharh: The moral of the last three lines: alarmed for a moment, people soon go back to living as if nothing had happened.

translation: Misery clings to the wretched,
who cannot turn it back when it comes.
194.sharh: Some people seem marked for misfortune, and nothing they do keeps it off. Al-Lakhmi and Ibn Khalawayh quote Imru' al-Qays: “Misery is poured out on the wretched.”

translation: Reproach keeps a free man straight and checks him;
a slave is checked by nothing but the stick.
195.sharh: A noble nature responds to a word of blame; a base one only to force. Al-Lakhmi and Ibn Khalawayh quote Ibn Mufarrigh's well-known line to the same effect.

translation: Passion is the blight of reason, and whoever's reason
rises above his passion is saved.
196.sharh: Desire undoes judgement; only a mind that masters it is safe. Ibn Khalawayh cites the Quran: “whoever feared standing before his Lord and held his soul back from desire, the Garden is his refuge.”

translation: Many a brother of displeasing ways
I have given my pure affection, out of a temper that pleases.
197.sharh: He has stood by many difficult friends, putting up with their faults. The next lines argue that no one is without them.

translation: Once you have tried a sword and found it good,
do not blame it on the day you see it glance aside.
198.sharh: A good sword may bounce off its target once; a proven friend may fail you once. Both lines rest on the proverb “every sharp sword glances aside, every good horse stumbles”.

translation: The thoroughbred takes the race, and yet at times
a stumble catches it in its stride and down it goes.
199.sharh: The second half of the proverb: the finest horse still falls sometimes, so judge friends by their record, not their slips.

translation: Who will find you the refined, ready man
to whom fault can find no way?
200.sharh: There is no such man. Al-Lakhmi and Ibn Khalawayh quote al-Nabigha: “You will keep no brother whose faults you do not bear: which man is flawless?”

translation: Search into people's lives and you will not
find a man who has reached perfection and has no need of more.
201.sharh: No one is perfect. Al-Lakhmi and Ibn Khalawayh quote the half-line “and who is it that is given perfection and is made whole?”

translation: Rely on fair patience: it is
the strongest refuge men of sense can turn to.
202.sharh: Lean on patience borne with dignity: it is the surest refuge of the wise. “Fair patience” is Jacob's phrase in the Quran when he hears of Joseph's fate. Al-Lakhmi says this line and the next are missing from most transmissions.

translation: Turn your soul to the ways of consolation
when the torment of grief unsettles your heart.
203.sharh: Comfort yourself with other people's sorrows. Usa, examples to follow, and asa, grief, again end the two halves, as in line 31.

translation: Time trips a man up, and at other times
it raises him from his fall when he has fallen.
204.sharh: Fortune turns both ways: one day it trips a man up, another it lifts him from his fall, so neither the fall nor the rescue is final.

translation: Do not wonder how one who perished fell;
wonder rather how one who is safe escaped.
205.sharh: In a world like this, ruin is the rule and survival the miracle: do not ask how a man came to fall, ask how anyone gets through unharmed.

translation: The stars of glory have set,
and its shadow, already shrinking, has drawn in further.
206.sharh: The great men who were the stars of their age have died out, and the shade of honour they cast keeps narrowing. Al-Lakhmi compares Labid: “Gone are those in whose shelter one could live.”

translation: All but a remnant of people
through whom the way of noble deeds is still followed.
207.sharh: A few still show the way. Al-Lakhmi traces the line to al-Khansa's elegy for her brother Sakhr, whom “guides follow, like a peak with a fire on top”.

translation: When stories draw out the news of them
it is like the scent of a meadow the dew has visited at dawn.
208.sharh: To tell of their deeds is to release a fragrance like a garden after the morning dew. The fragrance stands for the good name their deeds leave behind.

translation: No one who sits with them hears
in their gatherings an obscene word, or a foul one.
209.sharh: Their gatherings are clean: whoever sits with them never hears a coarse or obscene word. Al-Lakhmi's text has “mixes with them” for “sits with them”, and he says most transmissions lack the line.

translation: How sweet life would be if a man's death
would take from him the richest bribe.
210.sharh: Life would be sweet if death could be bribed to pass a man by. Al-Lakhmi's own text reads “death would take the highest bribes”, but he prefers the wording given here, which needs no poetic licence.

translation: Or if a man could wear his youth as finery all his life
and grey hair did not strip him of those jewels.
211.sharh: Life would also be sweet if a man could wear his youth like jewellery all his life. Instead grey hair strips it from him, as a thief strips a woman of her ornaments. Both wishes are impossible, as the next line says.

translation: Far from it: whatever is borrowed is reclaimed,
and in Time's disasters people find examples for consolation.
212.sharh: Life and youth are only on loan. Al-Lakhmi traces the thought to Labid: “Wealth and family are only things held in trust, and one day the trust must be returned.”

translation: Many a band of young men whom the phantom of sleep kept company by night,
and they kept company with sleep, their necks drooping,
213.sharh: A night journey: his young companions nod off in the saddle, heads drooping, sleep keeping them company like a fellow traveller.

translation: while the night had laid its breast on the empty wastes
and the camels were kicking up the sandgrouse's nests,
214.sharh: Night has settled heavily over the desert, like a camel kneeling, and the riders' camels scatter the nests of sandgrouse. Al-Lakhmi credits Imru' al-Qays with first giving the night a breast.

translation: in a place where no faint sound guides the ear
but the hooting of the owl or the echo,
215.sharh: The desert at night is so still that no sound leads the ear to any living soul: there is only the owl's hoot and the echo of one's own voice. Al-Lakhmi's text has “no sound is brought to the ear”.

translation: I went along with them on the night journey until
the saddle-gear tilted with the weak and witless one,
216.sharh: He kept pace with them until the feeblest of them fell asleep and started slipping off his saddle; the next line says what he told them.

translation: I told them: “Taking it easy ends
in weakness: press on, and you will praise the night march when it is over.”
217.sharh: He urges the sleepy riders on, putting into verse the old proverb “At dawn the travellers praise the night march”: the effort of the dark hours pays off when morning finds you far along the road.

translation: Many a desolate water, brimming full,
its stone facings tumbled, its rim caved in,
218.sharh: A deserted well in the desert, so long unused that its stone lining has fallen in and the water stands to the brim. He describes it before saying, two lines on, that he came to drink there.

translation: where the feathers round its edges looked like
gleaming arrowheads, thinned and whetted to be tempered,
219.sharh: Birds have used the water so long that their feathers lie all round it like steel arrowheads. Al-Lakhmi traces the image to al-A'sha.

translation: I came down to it while the wolf howled around it,
the holes of its ears shrunk shut from long hunger.
220.sharh: He drank there alone but for a wolf so starved it had gone deaf. Al-Lakhmi traces the scene to a poem of al-Najashi al-Harithi in which the poet talks with a wolf at a water.

translation: And many a begetter whose father's mother is his mother,
whose body was never thinned by the wasting of close kin,
221.sharh: A riddle about making fire with two sticks. Al-Lakhmi explains: the upper fire-stick was cut from a branch, its “father”, and the tree is mother to both branch and stick. Children of close relatives were thought to be born puny, but this “child” is not.

translation: I laid his brother's daughter under him, and she brought forth
a child by which fire is struck and meat is roasted.
222.sharh: The lower stick, cut from another branch of the same tree, is the upper stick's “niece”; rubbing them together produces fire. Al-Lakhmi traces the riddle to Dhu al-Rumma.

translation: And many a lookout peak, smooth on every side,
hard to approach and rough to climb,
223.sharh: Many a high, sheer lookout he has climbed, hard to reach and harder to scale; the line after next says when. A lookout was where a scout watched the desert for raiders.

translation: where a figure in the mirage shows to one who looks:
now you make it out, now it is lost to sight,
224.sharh: From the height, shapes on the plain waver in the mirage, appearing and vanishing. Neither commentator explains this line; Attar gives it in a note from some transmissions.

translation: I climbed it when the sun was spitting out its spittle
and the shadow was cut to the pattern of the sandal underfoot.
225.sharh: He climbed at high noon, when heat shimmers like threads falling from the sky (“the sun's spittle”) and a man's shadow has shrunk to the size of his sandal. Al-Lakhmi traces the shadow to al-Ajjaj.

translation: And many a night traveller to whom the wolf brings comfort
when the wolf writhes with hunger at nightfall and howls,
226.sharh: A lost traveller is glad to hear a wolf, which Ibn Khalawayh explains: wolves keep near flocks, so a howl means people are close by.

translation: made for my fire, and it is a place men know well,
whose light calls the needy to hospitality.
227.sharh: His fire was a beacon of generosity. Ibn Khalawayh says noble Arabs lit their fires on high ground so that the lost and the hungry could find them.

translation: How wondrous a visiting phantom
that dreams lead in to the heart like a bride.
228.sharh: The beloved's image visits him in a dream; dreams bring it to him as a bride is brought to her husband. Al-Lakhmi's text reads “to the eye”.

translation: It crosses the heart of the wastes, scorning
the terror of night's darkness when night comes on.
229.sharh: The phantom crosses the heart of the desert by night, scorning the darkness that frightens travellers. Distance and night are nothing to it: in a moment it covers the road that takes a caravan many nights.

translation: Ask it, if it could speak plainly of itself,
how it rode the night, or how it found its way,
230.sharh: He tells the listener to ask the phantom, if it could speak, how it rode through the night and found its way to him so far from home. Al-Lakhmi traces the question to Ali ibn Jabala's “How did you cross the breadth of a desert?”

translation: or whether it knew, before this, what Fars was,
and what its wastes were, its deserts and its villages.
231.sharh: The phantom has come to him in Fars, the Persian province where he lived with the Mikalis, a land it never knew. Al-Lakhmi notes that Fars, normally indeclinable, is declined here for the metre.

translation: And many a one asks me what drove me from a homeland
whose courts never grew narrow for me, nor turned me away.
232.sharh: Someone asks him why he left a homeland that never grew too narrow for him or turned him away. Ibn Khalawayh dwells on love of homeland and the Prophet's grief at leaving Mecca. The answer comes in the next line.

translation: I said: “Fate owns a man's affairs,
from where he does not know and from where he knows.”
233.sharh: His answer to the question is fate: fate rules a man's affairs and moves him, whether he sees it coming or not. He did not choose to leave his homeland; it was decreed.

translation: Don't ask me: ask Fate whether any stronghold
or any refuge on the heights protects a man from it.
234.sharh: Do not ask him; ask Fate whether any stronghold or mountain refuge can protect a man from it. There is no hiding from what is decreed. Wazar, “refuge”, recalls the Quran's “No refuge” on the Day of Judgement.

translation: A man cannot but meet what the Lord of the Throne
has written and set down of all he is to meet.
235.sharh: Everything a man meets was written for him beforehand; Ibn Khalawayh explains it as the Preserved Tablet, where all that happens is recorded.

translation: No wonder if an unjust Time persists
and strips the marrow-bone and picks out the marrow.
236.sharh: It is no surprise that cruel Time keeps at a man until it has taken his best. Ibn Khalawayh recalls the Prophet's warning not to curse Time, for it is God who acts.

translation: Yet you may see the withered tree turn green,
and meet the destitute one day grown rich.
237.sharh: Time can also give back: dead wood puts out leaves and the poor become rich. Al-Lakhmi and Ibn Khalawayh quote Abu Mihjan: “The stick puts on leaves again after drying.”

translation: O you women there, have you sought out for us
the one who pierced her veil for eyes like a fawn's?
238.sharh: He turns to love again, calling to the women of the camp about a girl whose eyes look out through her veil. Huliyya, “you dear little ones”, is a playful diminutive of “you there”.

translation: She was not fair, the mother of the two boys,
who made a sober man play the youth, when he was not one to be lured.
239.sharh: A mature, perfect woman has turned a grave man's head. Al-Lakhmi says “mother of the two boys” was a phrase of praise for such a woman; some took the “two boys” to be the pupils of her eyes.

translation: Be ashamed before the white at your temples
lest the white-skinned lead you as a blind man is led.
240.sharh: He scolds himself: grey hair should keep him from chasing women. Bid means both white hairs and fair women, and the line plays on the two.

translation: Far from it: how ugly a slip this is,
to be giddy after grey hair and a receding brow.
241.sharh: He rebukes himself: to be giddy with love once his hair is grey and his brow bare is an ugly lapse. Ibn Khalawayh: “The ugliest slips are a scholar's and an old man's.”

translation: Many a night has had its two ends drawn together for me
by a daughter of eighty, unveiled like a bride.
242.sharh: Old wine made the night pass in a flash. “Daughter of eighty” is wine, either because it was eighty years old or because drinkers were punished with eighty lashes; al-Lakhmi gives both.

translation: Water never got the better of her,
and no fanned fire ever sullied her.
243.sharh: The wine is drunk neat, never mixed with water to tame it, and was never boiled down over a fire as cheaper wines were: it is pure and strong. Al-Lakhmi traces the line to Abu Nuwas.

translation: At times she is the sickness, and at times in her
one finds the cure for her own sickness when it flares.
244.sharh: Wine causes the hangover and cures it, the paradox of Abu Nuwas's famous “Cure me with what was itself the disease”. Al-Lakhmi says this line and the next two are missing from most transmissions.

translation: The vintner kept her safe when he had chosen her,
too jealous of her to let others have her, and hid her away.
245.sharh: The vintner prized this wine above all his stock and kept it hidden, which is why it grew so old. Al-Lakhmi reads “chose her over the others”.

translation: So that, from her great age, when she appears
in her cup, she is all but invisible to men's eyes.
246.sharh: The old wine is so clear that the cup looks empty. Al-Lakhmi gives several readings of kala, among them “in a flash”.

translation: As if the sun's rim, rising,
took its lead from what she does in the bowl and the cup.
247.sharh: The wine glows so brightly in bowl and cup that the rim of the rising sun seems to be copying it: the wine outshines the dawn.

translation: I passed it back and forth with a splendid man whose fire
never turns on his companion when he is tipsy,
248.sharh: His drinking companion is a gentleman who never grows quarrelsome in his cups. Al-Lakhmi traces the line to Hassan ibn Thabit.

translation: the order of whose words is like the blossom of a meadow,
whether he improvises, or recites, or sings.
249.sharh: His drinking companion's words are as lovely as a meadow in flower, whether he speaks off the cuff, recites the poems of others or sings.

translation: Of all a young man can win, I have won my share,
and when a man is gone, what remains is the good that is said of him.
250.sharh: He has had everything life gives a man, and what outlasts a man is only the good that is said of him. Ibn Khalawayh records a reading with “report” for “praise”. Al-Lakhmi traces the first half to Zuhayr ibn Janab.

translation: If I die, my pleasures have run their course,
and everything that reaches its limit comes to an end.
251.sharh: He is ready for death: he has had his fill of life's pleasures, and everything comes to an end once it reaches its limit. There is nothing left for him to want.

translation: And if I live, I will keep company with my time, knowing
what its turns have folded away and what they have unfolded.
252.sharh: If he lives on, he will keep company with Time as one who knows it, aware both of what it hides and of what it brings into the open, so that nothing can take him by surprise.

translation: Far be it, for all that reason and forbearance have left in me,
that I should follow those who go out in search of filth,
253.sharh: The closing self-portrait: the reason and self-command that long experience has left him will keep him from following those who go looking for vice.

translation: or that I should be seen humbled by a calamity,
or, for some joy, exulting and puffed up.
254.sharh: The last line ends where the poem began, in steadiness: neither crushed by bad fortune nor carried away by good. Al-Lakhmi traces it to Mutammim ibn Nuwayra.

1.1.5.head: المَها
1.1.5.meaning: Maha: wild cows (the oryx), whose large dark eyes are the standard of beauty.

1.2.2.meaning: Khuzama: a sweet-smelling desert flower, lavender.

2.2.1.head: طُرَّة
2.2.1.meaning: Turra: the edge; here the first streak of dawn.

3.2.6.meaning: Ghada: a desert tree whose wood burns long and hot.

5.1.3.head: شِرَّة
5.1.3.meaning: Shirra: the vigour and fire of youth.

5.2.4.meaning: Jawa: the burning of love or grief.

8.2.4.head: طَيف
8.2.4.meaning: Tayf: the phantom of the beloved seen in sleep.

9.2.4.head: أَسأَرَ
9.2.4.meaning: Left over, as the dregs of a drink.

11.2.2.head: قُصارى
11.2.2.meaning: Qusara: its end, all it can come to.

12.1.1.head: شَجِيَ
12.1.1.meaning: I choked on something lodged in the throat.

12.2.5.meaning: Shaja: a bone lodged in the throat.

14.2.3.head: أَصمى
14.2.3.meaning: Would have killed me on the spot, a hunter's word for a clean kill.

15.2.3.head: أَرَب
15.2.3.meaning: Arab: need, or (for Ibn Khalawayh) intelligence.

16.1.1.head: شَيم
16.1.1.meaning: Shaym: watching for lightning in hope of rain.

16.1.3.head: خُلَّب
16.1.3.meaning: Khullab: lightning that brings no rain.

17.1.5.head: مُستَوبِل
17.1.5.meaning: Mustawbil: unhealthy, disagreeing with one's body.

18.2.1.head: ضَرّاء
18.2.1.meaning: Darra': hardship. Ibn Khalawayh reads sarra', solid rock.

18.2.5.head: ضَبّ
18.2.5.meaning: Dabb: a desert lizard that lives in hard ground.

19.2.5.meaning: Muntasha: drinking to the last drop. Al-Lakhmi reads muntasa, what lies far off.

22.1.4.head: أَنصَبَ
22.1.4.meaning: You have tired me out. Al-Lakhmi and Ibn Khalawayh read andaytani, you have worn me thin.

23.2.2.head: عَرَقَ
23.2.2.meaning: Strips me, as meat is stripped from a bone.

25.1.3.head: مَصدور
25.1.3.meaning: Masdur: one sick in the chest; the proverb says he cannot help spitting.

25.2.2.head: لُغام
25.2.2.meaning: Lugham: the froth on a camel's mouth.

25.2.5.meaning: Ghama: covered over. Al-Lakhmi and Ibn Khalawayh read ama, threw it off.

27.1.2.head: الجَديدان
27.1.2.meaning: The two new ones: night and day, forever renewed.

30.2.5-6.meaning: La la'a: “no rising”, refusing the wish la'an, “up you get”, said to one who stumbles.

31.2.3.meaning: Usa: examples to take comfort from.

32.1.2-3.meaning: Imru' al-Qays ibn Hujr of Kinda, the great pre-Islamic poet. He sought the Byzantine emperor's help to avenge his father and regain his kingdom, and died at Ankara on the way back; the story is that the emperor sent him a poisoned robe.

33.1.3-4.meaning: Abu al-Jabr: a king of Kinda, poisoned by the Persian horsemen the Persian king gave him; he died on his way back to Yemen.

34.1.1-2.head: اِبن الأَشَجّ
34.1.1-2.meaning: Ibn al-Ashajj: Abd al-Rahman ibn Muhammad ibn al-Ash'ath of Kinda (al-Ashajj, “the scarred”, was his ancestor's nickname), who led the great revolt against al-Hajjaj, the Umayyad governor of Iraq.

34.1.3.head: القَيل
34.1.3.meaning: Qayl: a prince, a Yemeni king below the great king.

35.1.2.head: الوَضّاح
35.1.2.meaning: Al-Waddah, “the shining one”: Jadhima al-Abrash, an early Arab king of al-Hira, so called because people dared not name his leprosy; al-Zabba' killed him to avenge her father.

36.1.4.meaning: Yazid ibn al-Muhallab of Azd, a famous Umayyad general. He escaped from prison, took Basra and rose against the caliph Yazid ibn Abd al-Malik, and was killed fighting the caliph's brother Maslama.

37.2.1-3.meaning: “Gravity grew grave with him”: matters turned deadly serious.

38.1.3.head: بِدع
38.1.3.meaning: Bid': the first of his kind, an exception.

38.1.5.head: عَرانين
38.1.5.meaning: Aranin: noses, hence chiefs, the nobility.

39.2.3.head: أَلا
39.2.3.meaning: Lam alu: I will not fall short.

39.2.6.meaning: Tha'a: a rift, damage to be mended.

40.1.3.meaning: Amr ibn Adi of Lakhm, Jadhima's nephew and successor as king of al-Hira and the first of the Lakhmid kings, who avenged him on al-Zabba'.

40.1.5.head: أَوتار
40.1.5.meaning: Awtar: blood-debts, wrongs to be avenged.

41.1.2.head: الزَّبّاء
41.1.2.meaning: Al-Zabba': the queen of al-Jazira and the Syrian marches who killed Jadhima; Amr and Qasir trapped her and she took poison. Some identify her with Zenobia of Palmyra.

41.2.2.head: لوح
41.2.2.meaning: Luh: the open air between earth and sky.

42.1.1.head: سَيف
42.1.1.meaning: Sayf ibn Dhi Yazan, a prince of Himyar who drove the Abyssinians out of Yemen with Persian help, then ruled it until his Abyssinian servants killed him.

43.2.3.head: غُمدان
43.2.3.meaning: Ghumdan: a great palace at San'a, said to be Sayf's; al-Lakhmi and Ibn Khalawayh say the caliph Uthman demolished it.

43.2.4.head: مِحراب
43.2.4.meaning: Mihrab: here the upper chamber, the seat of honour.

44.1.2-3.head: اِبن هِند
44.1.2-3.meaning: Ibn Hind: Amr ibn al-Mundhir, king of al-Hira (Hind was his mother), nicknamed “the Burner”.

44.2.2.head: أُوارات
44.2.2.meaning: Uwarat: the Day of Uwara, a famous battle-day; Uwara was a hill or well of Tamim.

48.2.3.head: الآل
48.2.3.meaning: Al: the mirage that shimmers on the desert, seeming to lift shapes off the ground.

51.2.2-3.head: قِدح النَّبع
51.2.2-3.meaning: “An arrow-shaft of nab'”: an unfeathered shaft of nab', the hard mountain wood used for the best bows and arrows.

54.2.3.head: المَروَتان
54.2.3.meaning: “The two Marwas”: al-Safa and al-Marwa, the two hills between which pilgrims walk.

55.2.5.head: لَبّى
55.2.5.meaning: Answered God's call: “Here I am, O God, here I am.”

56.2.3.head: المَأزِمان
56.2.3.meaning: The two Ma'zims: two hills between Muzdalifa and Arafat.

56.2.4.head: مِنى
56.2.4.meaning: Mina: the valley near Mecca where pilgrims stone the pillars.

57.1.3.head: التَّعريف
57.1.3.meaning: Ta'rif: Arafat, the plain where pilgrims stand in prayer.

57.2.3.head: أَلال
57.2.3.meaning: Alal (or Ilal): a hill at Arafat where the imam stands.

58.2.5.head: الصُّوى
58.2.5.meaning: Suwa: cairns, waymarks on high ground.

59.1.2.head: تَوديع
59.1.2.meaning: The farewell circuit of the Ka'ba.

61.2.2.head: الحَماليق
61.2.2.meaning: Hamaliq: the inner eyelids; a sidelong look was prized in a horse as a sign of spirit.

63.2.5.meaning: Mustala: where one stands to warm oneself at a fire.

64.1.5.head: قِرن
64.1.5.meaning: Qirn: a match in single combat.

67.1.3.head: الشُّمّ
